t: An oracle: a message that is lifted
p: Massa' is the Hebrew heading word; it means a weighty word, spoken against or about a nation.
b: The Hebrew is massa', from nasa', "lift up": a lifting up of the voice, or a load laid on the hearer. The King James Version has "burden"; this Plain English Translation says "oracle," as it does at Isaiah 13:1 and Proverbs 30:1. The same heading opens Habakkuk 1:1 and Malachi 1:1 and marks messages aimed at a nation. The Greek here simply writes the Greek word lemma ("that which is taken"), a sign that its translators also took the word as a technical heading. Jeremiah 23:33-40 plays on both senses, "oracle" and "load." Nahum is the only prophet whose whole book is one oracle against one city, and it is addressed to Nineveh, though the first hearers were most likely Judeans (see the book's audience).
r: Isaiah 13:1; Proverbs 30:1; Jeremiah 23:33; Habakkuk 1:1; Malachi 1:1; Jonah 1:2

p: The name means "comfort." No one knows where Elkosh was; several places have been proposed.
b: Nachum comes from nacham, "comfort," the root also in the name Nehemiah ("the LORD comforts"). The book plays on the name (see 3:7). Nothing else is known about the man. Where was Elkosh? Jerome, in the preface to his commentary on Nahum (written about AD 392), says that Elcesi was still a small village in Galilee, barely showing the ruins of old buildings but known to the Jews, and that a guide showed it to him. Calvin, in his lecture on 1:1, says Jerome records a village of that name in the tribe of Simeon. Jerome's preface does not say that; Simeon is where the Lives of the Prophets puts it, so Calvin seems to have mixed the two traditions. A tomb said to be Nahum's is shown at Alqosh in northern Iraq, near Nineveh. Others say a village in southern Judah, or link Capernaum, "Village of Nahum," with him. The Lives of the Prophets, a late Jewish-Christian work, puts Elkesei in the tribe of Simeon. Each is a later guess, and the commonest scholarly answer is that the place is unknown. The Plain English Translation keeps "of Elkosh" and does not choose.

a: The LORD is a jealous God
p: Hebrew lines in 1:2-8 begin with successive letters of the alphabet, but the pattern breaks. Scholars disagree.
b: In 1893 Hermann Gunkel saw that lines of 1:2-8 open with the first letters of the Hebrew alphabet, starting with aleph in 'El ("God") and going on, with gaps, toward the middle of the alphabet. Duane Christensen (1975) reworked the pattern. For: a hymn that opens with the alphabet is a known form (Psalms 9-10, 25, 34, 111, 112, 119, 145; Lamentations). Against: the pattern stops, some letters are missing, and fitting the rest takes repeated changes to the Hebrew; many recent commentators (Roberts, Spronk and others) call it at best partial and a poor base for rewriting the text. The Plain English Translation does not rewrite for the pattern. The hymn also seems to have been joined to the oracle in 1:9-15, which is a separate question (see the chapter page).

p: Qanno' is the word of a spouse's loyalty; it does not mean envy.
b: Qanno' (and qin'ah) means a zeal that will not share what is its own. It is the word used when the LORD says no other god may stand beside him (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24; 5:9; 6:15), and the Plain English Translation says "jealous" in each. It is the passion of a husband or covenant partner who will not be betrayed, and Song of Songs 8:6 uses the noun for love that is "strong as death." So the word carries both warmth and threat. Here it is joined to noqem ("takes vengeance") and to the shelter of 1:7: the jealousy that fights Nineveh is the same loyalty that protects those who trust him. The Greek has zelotes, from which comes "zealot."
r: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24; Joshua 24:19; Song of Songs 8:6

t: Vengeance: a judge setting things right
p: Naqam is a legal word. In the Bible it is mostly God's right, and a call to leave vengeance to him.
b: Naqam ("take vengeance," "avenge") is the act of someone with authority who puts a wrong right and pays it back. The Plain English Translation uses "vengeance" as in Deuteronomy 32:35, 41 and Psalm 94:1 ("God who takes vengeance"). The word is used for a king's or a champion's justice, not only anger. The verse has the word three times in the Hebrew (as the Plain English Translation does), and no "is," which gives a drumbeat. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 in Romans 12:19 to tell Christians not to take vengeance but to leave it to God, so the same word that frightens a city also restrains the believer. The book of Nahum never tells Judah to take vengeance; it tells Judah to keep its festivals (1:15).

t: Lord of rage: who holds the reins?
p: Ba'al chemah, literally 'owner of rage,' can mean one who rules his anger or one who is full of it.
b: Ba'al means "owner" or "master of," as in "master of dreams" (Genesis 37:19). "Owner of rage" can mean full of rage, but it can equally mean one who has rage under control and uses it when he chooses. The second sense fits the next verse, where the same God is "slow to anger." The Greek has "the LORD with wrath." The Plain English Translation's "is his to wield" leaves both senses open. The point for the reader is that the Hebrew pictures anger as a power God holds, not a mood that holds him.

p: Noter is the verb used for a human grudge in Leviticus; for God it is reserved judgment.
b: Natar means to keep or guard. In Leviticus 19:18 people are told not to "bear a grudge" with this verb. Psalm 103:9 says the LORD does not keep (natar) his anger forever. Nahum says that for his enemies he does keep it, for the time being. The tension is plain: the God who forbids grudges keeps anger. One answer is that God's keeping is judicial: he waits, as a judge waits, and does not strike in a fit. Calvin, in his lecture on 1:2, takes the word as vengeance stored up for the unbelieving and for those who despise God. The Plain English Translation avoids "grudge," which would shrink the picture.

a: The LORD is slow to anger
t: The creed turned: Nahum, Joel and Jonah
p: Nahum quotes the creed of Exodus 34:6-7 but drops the mercy and keeps the warning.
b: The creed God speaks at Sinai (Exodus 34:6-7: "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness ... Yet he will by no means leave guilt unpunished") is quoted in the Twelve in Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2 and Nahum 1:3, and is echoed in part in Micah 7:18-20. Joel and Jonah take the mercy half, with changes from Exodus: they reverse the first pair ("gracious and compassionate"), drop "and faithfulness," and add "changes his mind about the harm." Nahum 1:3 takes only "slow to anger," puts "great of power" (the Plain English Translation: "his power is great") where Joel and Jonah have "great in loyal love," and then gives the second half of Exodus 34:7. Differences from Exodus: no compassion, no grace, no loyal love, no faithfulness, no changing of his mind. Jonah, set a century or more before Nahum, ends with a God who spares Nineveh; Nahum says the same God does not leave guilt unpunished. The two books use the same creed to say what happened to the same city at two different times.
r: Exodus 34:6; Exodus 34:7; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Micah 7:18; Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Nehemiah 9:17

a: he will by no means leave guilt unpunished
p: The Hebrew repeats the verb (naqeh lo yenaqqeh), as in Exodus 34:7, where the Plain English Translation supplies "guilt."
b: The Hebrew is venaqqeh lo yenaqqeh, the same words as Exodus 34:7. The verb naqah means "be clean, go free"; with a negative it means "leave unpunished." The Plain English Translation follows its own Exodus 34:7 wording ("he will by no means leave guilt unpunished"), adding the object "guilt" because the Hebrew has none and the sense needs one. The alternative is "the guilty" (a person). The Hebrew has no object in either book, so the two Plain English Translation readings match on purpose. In Exodus the clause follows the whole list of mercies; here it comes right after "slow to anger" and "his power is great." The meaning of "slow" is that punishment is delayed, not that it never comes.

a: He goes his way in gale and storm
t: The storm God and the LORD
p: Storm imagery was shared with Israel's neighbors, but Israel says the LORD alone commands the storm.
b: In Syria, Canaan and Mesopotamia the storm was a god's weapon: Baal (Hadad, Adad) on his clouds, thunder as his voice. The LORD in Israel's poetry also rides the storm and the clouds (Psalm 18:7-15; Psalm 29; Habakkuk 3:3-15; Job 38:1). Is there a link? The images overlap, and Kevin Cathcart (1973) compared Nahum's wording with the poems of Ugarit, the Canaanite city whose texts were found in 1929. The honest verdict is that the images are shared across the region; what is different is the claim, that the LORD, not Baal, commands the storm, and that he is a judge of nations. Nahum may have chosen the picture to answer the Assyrian claim that Ashur or Adad did; that is an inference, and the text does not say so.

t: He scolds the sea and the rivers
p: The sea and the rivers dry at the LORD's word, as at the Exodus and at the Jordan.
b: The verb ga'ar is "scold" or "rebuke," a strong command to stop. The Plain English Translation says "scolds" as it does at Psalm 106:9 ("He scolded the Sea of Reeds, and it went dry"), Psalm 104:7 and Isaiah 17:13. The waters of Exodus 14:21 and the Jordan of Joshua 3:16 stop as the Israelites cross, and Isaiah 50:2 repeats the picture. In Canaanite stories the Sea is a rival that the storm god defeats. Israel's poetry has it both ways: the Sea obeys (Psalm 89:9: "master of the sea when it swells") and is also an enemy God breaks (Psalm 74:13). The picture here is the Exodus turned against the empire: the power that dried the sea for Israel will dry the rivers, including the rivers of Nineveh and its canals (see 2:6). In Mark 4:39 Jesus "spoke sternly to the wind and said to the sea, 'Quiet! Be muzzled!'" The Greek verb there is epitimao, which the Greek of Psalm 106:9 uses for ga'ar; the Greek of Nahum 1:4 has "threatening" (apeilon), see the variant.
r: Exodus 14:21; Joshua 3:16; Psalm 106:9; Psalm 104:7; Psalm 89:9; Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 50:2; Isaiah 17:13; Mark 4:39

p: These were the three greenest places in Israel's world. When they wither, nothing is safe.
b: Bashan (east of the Sea of Galilee) was cattle country, Carmel (the headland by the Mediterranean) was wooded and rainy, and Lebanon had the cedars. Together they stood for lush growth. The prophets say they dry up when the LORD comes in judgment (Isaiah 33:9; Amos 1:2 for Carmel), and bloom when he restores (Isaiah 35:2). The same Hebrew word, 'umlal, "withers," is used twice in the verse; the Greek uses two different verbs ("was made few" and "failed"). The Plain English Translation keeps the repeat.

a: Who can stand up when he is indignant?
p: The Hebrew has indignation (za'am), burning anger ('af charon) and rage (chemah), kept apart in the Plain English Translation.
b: Verse 6 piles up three of the Bible's anger words: za'am ("indignation," the anger of a judge at a wrong), 'af charon ("burning anger," literally "the burning of the nose") and chemah ("rage," literally "heat"). The Plain English Translation uses "indignant," "burning anger" and "rage" and keeps them apart across the book, as in Lamentations. The Greek uses orge and thymos for them. The rhetorical question "Who can stand?" is also asked in Malachi 3:2 and in Revelation 6:17 ("the great day of their anger is here, and who is able to stand?"), and Joel 2:11 asks "who can endure it?"
orig: זַעַם, חֲרוֹן אַף, חֵמָה (za'am, charon 'af, chemah)

t: The one comfort in the hymn
p: Verse 7 stands between the storm and the flood, and readers have asked how the two fit.
b: Verses 2-6 and 8 are about wrath; verse 7 is about shelter. The same coming that wrecks the mountains is a refuge for some. Calvin, in his lecture on 1:7, reads the verse as the prophet's answer to the charge that God is too severe: the LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and the threats of the hymn do not cancel his goodness to those who hope in him. Medieval Jewish commentators are reported to read it as shelter for Judah while Assyria falls; none is named here, because none was checked. Modern readers see the verse as the hinge of the poem: the choice is between taking shelter in the LORD and standing against him. It echoes Psalm 34:8 and 46:1 and sets the tone for Nahum's answer to Jonah (see 3:19). The Greek has no "stronghold" and reads "those who revere him" (see the variant).

p: The Hebrew has a feminine "her" with no stated owner. The Greek has a different word.
b: The Hebrew meqomah means "her place" (the suffix is feminine). The only feminine thing near is Nineveh in the next verses, or the city in general; some think of the "place" of the LORD's temple; a few suggest an earlier word dropped out. The Greek reads "those who rise up against him" (see the variant). Mur88 has the same letters as the Masoretic Text. The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew as it is and does not add "Nineveh" here, since the book names Nineveh only in 1:1, 2:8 and 3:7.

t: The flood and the fall of Nineveh
p: A flood is the picture of an invading army. Later writers also tell of a real flood at Nineveh.
b: "Flood" is a common prophetic picture for an army sweeping across land (Isaiah 8:7-8; Jeremiah 47:2; Daniel 9:26). In Nahum the river and water images return in 2:6 (the river gates), 2:8 (the pool) and 3:8 (Thebes' water walls). The Babylonian chronicle on the fall of Nineveh (the "Fall of Nineveh Chronicle," ABC 3) reports that the Babylonians and Medes besieged the city for about three months in 612 BC, defeated a great people, and carried off the city's treasure. Diodorus Siculus (writing in the first century BC, from the Greek Ctesias) tells that the Tigris flooded and broke down part of the wall. That is a late story and is not a source for the Plain English Translation. Whether Nahum had a real flood in mind is debated.

a: What are you plotting against the LORD?
t: Who is speaking, and to whom? (1:9-14)
p: The "you" shifts, and in 1:14 it is masculine, not feminine. The Plain English Translation keeps the changes.
b: In 1:9-14 the Hebrew shifts between "you" (plural, 1:9), "he" (a plotter, 1:11, 13-14), "they" (1:10, 12), and "you" (singular). The singular "you" changes gender. It is feminine in 1:11-13 (mimmekh, 'innitikh, me'alayikh, mosrotayikh) and again in 1:15 (nedarayikh, bakh), and both Nineveh (2:1; 3:5) and Judah (1:15) are addressed as feminine elsewhere in the book. In 1:14 it is masculine ('alekha, mishimkha, 'elohekha, qivrekha, qallota). That masculine "you" ("your name," "your gods," "your grave") does not fit a feminine city or people; it is addressed to a man, most naturally the Assyrian king or the worthless adviser of 1:11 and 1:15. Sometimes the LORD speaks (1:12-14), and sometimes the prophet speaks about him (1:9, 14a). There are two main solutions for the rest. (1) The addressee is Nineveh (or Assyria) in 1:9-11 and Judah in 1:12-13 and 15, as the LORD turns from one to the other, with a king addressed in 1:14. (2) The whole section is addressed to Judah or to one group in it, and "he" is an Assyrian king. The Plain English Translation does not label the speaker and lets the reader see the turn, as the Hebrew does. The oracle is a mix of taunt and comfort in all views.

p: Beliyya'al is the Plain English Translation's "worthless." It is used again in 1:15, so the schemer of 1:11 is the one cut off in 1:15.
b: Beliyya'al is rendered "worthless" across the Plain English Translation (as in Deuteronomy 13:13 and Judges 19:22). The "worthless adviser" (yo'ets beliyya'al) is a counselor of no value, and probably of harm. Who is he? Some commentators think of Sennacherib, whose messengers spoke against the LORD and Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17-35; Isaiah 36:4-20; compare Isaiah 37:23); others think of the Assyrian king in general, or of Assyria's whole policy of conquest. The Greek has no name or title here: "a plan against the LORD will come out of you, plotting hostile evils" (see the variant). The word returns in 1:15, "the worthless one will never again pass through you," so the one who plots in 1:11 and the one who is cut off in 1:15 are the same.

p: The feminine singular "you" is not named. Most take it as Judah, a few as Nineveh.
b: The verb 'anah means "bring low" or "humble" and is also used for oppression (Exodus 1:11-12). Judah: the commonest view. The LORD used Assyria to bring Judah low (Isaiah 10:5-6; 2 Kings 17-18; the tribute of 2 Kings 18:14-16), and now he says it is over. This fits 1:13 (the yoke is taken off "you") and 1:15 ("Judah"). Nineveh: the LORD has humbled Nineveh before and will not need to again, because the next blow is final. The Greek has no "I have brought you low" (see the variant). The masculine "you" of 1:14 is a separate question (see the note at 1:9). The Plain English Translation leaves the "you" of 1:12 without a name.

t: The verb "pass over" (avar) through the book
p: The Hebrew verb avar returns in 1:8, 1:12, 1:15 and 3:19. It ties the flood to the end.
b: 'Avar, "pass over, pass through, pass on," shows up at four key points. In 1:8 the flood "passes over" (Plain English Translation: "sweeping over"); in 1:12 the plotter "passes on" (or "passes away"); in 1:15 the worthless one will not again "pass through" Judah; in 3:19 Nineveh's wickedness has "passed over" everyone. Isaiah 8:8 uses the same verb for the Assyrian flood passing through Judah. The word works as a thread: Assyria passed through the nations as a flood; now a flood passes over Assyria. The Plain English Translation keeps "pass" in 1:12, 1:15 and 3:19, and "sweeping over" in 1:8, since English does not allow one verb in all four places.

p: Judah paid tribute to Assyria for about a century. Esarhaddon's list names Manasseh among those who served.
b: A "yoke" is a tribute and service burden. Ahaz asked for Assyria's help and paid (2 Kings 16:7-8); Hezekiah paid heavily after 701 BC (2 Kings 18:14-16). Isaiah promised that Assyria's yoke would come off (Isaiah 10:27; 14:25). Texts from Assyria itself confirm the situation: Esarhaddon's Prism B (about 673 BC) lists "Manasseh, king of Judah" among twenty-two kings of Hatti, the western lands, who supplied materials for his building works (Ancient Near Eastern Texts, 3rd ed., p. 291), and a prism of Ashurbanipal lists him again. Whether the Nahum oracle belongs to Manasseh's long reign (when the yoke was heaviest) or to the weakening Assyria of Josiah's early years (see the book's date) is debated. Josiah's reforms (2 Kings 22-23) may show Judah acting without Assyrian leave; that is an inference, since the text does not say whether Assyria allowed them.

a: Nothing more will be sown from your name
p: To "sow" a name means to have descendants who carry it on. The line of Assyria's kings will end.
b: The Hebrew lo yizzare' mishimkha 'od is literally "it will not be sown from your name again." Seed carries a family on, as in Isaiah 14:20-22, where Babylon's "name and remnant" are cut off. Psalm 109:13 prays that a wicked man's name be erased by the next generation. For an ancient king, the end of the line was a worse death than death itself. The verse speaks of a dynasty, and the Hebrew "you" is masculine here (see the note at 1:9), which suits a king. The final Assyrian kings are known by name (see 3:18): Ashur-uballit II made his last stand at Harran until about 609 BC (the Babylonian Chronicle), and no later king ruled Assyria.
orig: לֹא יִזָּרַע מִשִּׁמְךָ עוֹד (lo yizzara' mishimkha 'od)

a: the carved idol and the cast idol
p: The idols are the gods of Assyria's temples, such as the Ishtar of Nineveh, the empire's protectors.
b: The pair pesel and massekhah ("carved image and cast image") is the Bible's usual term for idols (Deuteronomy 27:15). Assyria's gods included Ashur (whose chief temple stood in the city of Ashur), the Ishtar of Nineveh and Nabu, and the last two had temples in Nineveh itself. Sennacherib was murdered by his sons while he was "bowing down in the house of Nisroch his god" (2 Kings 19:37). The Babylonian Chronicle says the conquerors carried off the vast spoil of the city and the temple. The warning in Nahum is that the gods Assyria prayed to would not hold the city. Compare Isaiah 37:12 and 37:19, where Assyria's boast that it burned the gods of other peoples is turned back on it.

p: The Hebrew Bible starts its chapter 2 here. English 2:1-13 is Hebrew 2:2-14, and chapter 3 matches.
b: This verse is Nahum 2:1 in the Hebrew Bible (and in Jewish Bibles). In Swete's Greek, chapter 1 runs on to "pass through you," and only the last words, "It is finished, it is taken away" (the Greek for "He is cut off completely"), begin Greek chapter 2 (see the variant). Hebrew chapter 1 therefore has 14 verses, chapter 2 has 14, and chapter 3 has 19. English chapter 1 has 15 verses and chapter 2 has 13. This Plain English Translation follows the English numbers throughout, and the notes give the Hebrew number where it matters. The mountains are probably the mountains of Judah, the messenger's way home. In the Hebrew numbering the chapter that begins here opens with news of peace for Judah, and the English chapter 2 with the attacker.

a: the one who brings good news
p: The words match Isaiah 52:7 almost exactly. Paul in Romans 10:15 adapts Isaiah's Greek; he does not quote Nahum.
b: The Hebrew mevasser mashmia' shalom, "one who brings news, who makes peace heard," is the same in Nahum 1:15 and Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah adds "good" and "salvation" and "your God is King." The Plain English Translation matches its Isaiah 52:7 wording ("the feet of the one who brings good news, who makes peace heard"). Which came first? Nahum is usually dated in the 600s BC and Isaiah 40-55 in the 500s, so some say Isaiah borrowed; others see a shared stock of heralds' phrases (2 Samuel 18:19-27 has messengers running with news). The New Testament verse is Romans 10:15, which is Paul's short adaptation of Isaiah 52:7, close to the Greek of Isaiah, and not a quotation of Nahum. Paul has the plural, "the feet of those who bring the good news of good things" (ton euangelizomenon ta agatha); the Greek of Isaiah has the singular (euangelizomenou, euangelizomenos agatha). Nahum's Greek has the same verb, euangelizomenou. The Plain English Translation's "good news" renders the Hebrew verb basar. The Greek Bible translates basar with euangelizomai, a Greek verb built from eu, "good," and angelos, "messenger," and the New Testament's "gospel" (euangelion) belongs to that Greek family. The English word "gospel" comes from Old English godspel, "good story," and has no link to basar.

t: The herald runs with news of battle
p: In ancient war a runner carried the result. Bad news and good news used the same word.
b: Basar means "bring news" and is used for good news and bad (1 Samuel 4:17 for defeat; 2 Samuel 4:10; 18:19-27, where two runners, Ahimaaz and a Cushite, bring word of Absalom's death). A watchman saw the runner from afar and judged by his running whether the news was good (2 Samuel 18:27). Judah's herald crosses the mountains with word that Assyria's rule is over; "peace" (shalom) is the end of war and the return of well-being. Paul applies the Isaiah wording to preachers of the gospel (Romans 10:15). Calvin, in his lecture on Nahum 1:15, reads the herald as the heralds of peace who may now speak freely on the mountains, because Assyria's rule has ended; he joins the verse to Isaiah's "How beautiful are the feet," and says the "wicked one" is Assyria and not the later Chaldeans. Other commentators on the herald were not checked for this edition.

t: Festivals and vows after the yoke
p: Pilgrim feasts needed the road to Jerusalem to be safe. Vows made in trouble were paid when it ended.
b: Chaggi chaggayikh is "keep festivals your festivals": the verb and the noun share a root (chag, a pilgrim feast). With the Assyrian army gone, Judeans could go up to Jerusalem again for Passover, Weeks and Booths (Deuteronomy 16). Josiah's great Passover (2 Kings 23:21-23) is a possible background. A vow made in a crisis was paid after deliverance (Psalm 66:13-14; Jonah 2:9; Jonah 1:16). The command "pay your vows" says the trouble is over, so the herald's message is a call to worship, not only a news report.

p: Mefits is a rare word, "one who scatters" or "smashes." The Greek has "one who blows" instead.
b: Mefits comes from puts, "scatter, break up." The noun may mean a hammer or club (a related form in Proverbs 25:18 is a "club") or an army that scatters its enemies. The Greek has emphysao, "one who blows in your face," reading a different Hebrew word (see the variant). The attacker is not named. The common historical answer is the Babylonians and the Medes (612 BC); Nahum himself says only that the LORD sends him, and some read the title as God's own, the one who scatters (Jeremiah 51:20 calls Babylon the LORD's war club). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and does not name the army.

t: The fall of Nineveh in 612 BC
p: The commands to the defenders are ironic. The Babylonian Chronicle gives the date and the attackers.
b: The four commands (guard, watch, brace yourselves, gather strength; the Hebrew for the third is "strengthen the loins") are a defender's drill, and the taunt is that none of it will help. The Babylonian Chronicle on the fall of Nineveh (ABC 3, "the Fall of Nineveh Chronicle") tells the story year by year: Nabopolassar of Babylon took the throne in 626 BC; the Medes took Ashur in 614; the Medes and Babylonians together besieged Nineveh in the summer of 612 and sacked it; the Assyrian army made a last stand at Harran until about 609. Josiah of Judah died at Megiddo in 609 after going out to meet Pharaoh Neco, who was marching up toward the king of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29; compare 2 Chronicles 35:20-24). Why Josiah went out is not stated in Kings; that he meant to stop Neco from helping Assyria is a probable inference. The Plain English Translation does not take the Chronicle as a source of the text; it reads Nahum's words as written, and the Chronicle as the historical background.

p: Does the promise name two groups, Judah (Jacob) and the northern kingdom (Israel), or one people twice?
b: The Hebrew says the LORD will restore "the pride of Jacob like the pride of Israel." Two groups: Jacob is Judah, and "Israel" is the northern kingdom taken by Assyria in 722-721 BC; the promise is that Judah's glory will return as Israel's once stood. One people: both names mean the whole covenant people, a poetic pair (as in Isaiah 14:1; Micah 1:5). A comparison: the "pride" (ga'on) of Jacob was something the LORD gave and loved (Psalm 47:4), and Amos 6:8 has the LORD say he loathes "the pride of Jacob," so the word could be good or bad. The Greek takes the word the second way and says he "turned away" the pride (see the variant). The Plain English Translation keeps "pride" and "bring back."
orig: גְּאוֹן יַעֲקֹב כִּגְאוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל (ge'on Ya'aqov kige'on Yisra'el)

p: The ruined branches picture the ruin of Judah's land. Sennacherib boasted of what he did there in 701 BC.
b: Israel was often pictured as a vine (Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; Hosea 10:1; Jeremiah 2:21), and its branches (zemorot) are its people or its land. In 701 BC Sennacherib's army overran the towns of Judah. His own account says he shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage" and counts forty-six walled towns taken. The word-play in the Hebrew, boqeqim baqaqum, "the emptiers have emptied them," is the first of the book's "empty" plays (the root returns in 2:10; compare Isaiah 24:1). The Plain English Translation has "Those who strip have stripped them bare," which keeps the repeated root.

a: The chariots glitter like fire with their metal
t: Peladot: a word found only here
p: Peladot is not known elsewhere. Guesses: steel, metal fittings, torches or flashing blades.
b: The Hebrew phrase is be'esh peladot ha-rekhev, "in fire of peladot the chariotry." The word occurs only here. Proposals: "steel" (by comparison with a later Persian-Arabic word for steel, fulad; the comparison is debated), "metal fittings," "torches," or "flashing blades." The Greek has "reins" (heniai), and either guessed or read a different word. The Plain English Translation's "fire with their metal" tries to keep the sense of glitter on the chariots. Two other puzzles in the verse are in the variants: the shields "dyed red" and the "cypress spears." The picture, as the whole verse shows, is of an army in its colors, seen from the walls.

a: He calls his great men to mind
p: The verb has no named subject. It is the king of Nineveh, or the attacking commander.
b: Yizkor 'adiraw is "he remembers his nobles." Nineveh's king: he summons his best men, but they stumble on the way to the wall. This is the usual reading. The attacker: the commander of the besiegers calls up his picked troops, who run to the wall (the verb "stumble" then means they trip in their haste). The Hebrew word for "nobles" ('adir, "the splendid") returns for Assyria's "great men" in 3:18. The Greek (see the variant) has them flee by day. The Plain English Translation keeps the unnamed "he" and the reader sees the haste either way.

a: The gates on the rivers swing open
p: Nineveh sat on the Tigris with canals brought in. Later writers tell of a flood that broke the wall.
b: The wall around Nineveh was cut by gates, and the city lay on the Tigris with canals brought in by Sennacherib. The "gates of the rivers" may have been the water gates and sluices that controlled these canals, or the Hebrew may speak figuratively of an enemy that pours in like a river. Diodorus Siculus (first century BC, from the Greek Ctesias) said a flood of the Tigris broke part of the wall; the text is late, and it is not part of the Plain English Translation's reading. The Greek has "gates of the cities" (see the variant). Some suggest the "palace" that "caves in" was mud brick weakened by water. That is a modern suggestion.

a: she is uncovered and carried off
t: Uncovered: the verb that also means exile
p: Galah means both "uncover" and "go into exile." The same verb is used for the nakedness of 3:5.
b: Gulletah is from galah, which in the Hebrew means "uncover, reveal" and "go into exile" (a people "uncovered" of its home). Both meanings are at work: the woman Nineveh is stripped (as in 3:5, where the cognate verb says "I will uncover your skirts") and carried off as a captive. The second verb, he'ultah, is the hophal of 'alah and means "was brought up" or "was led up"; "carried off" is the Plain English Translation's reading of it as being led away into exile, which is an interpretation. The pair "uncovered and led up" (gulletah he'ultah) is read two ways by the ancient versions: as a woman led up to be shamed, or as an image (the queen carried away). Isaiah 47:3 uses the same verb for Babylon's nakedness. The Plain English Translation keeps "uncovered" so the link to 3:5 stays visible; the other sense is in this note.

p: Assyria grew rich on loot. The commands to loot are the same word as the plunder in 3:1.
b: Bazaz is "loot, plunder." The prophets said again and again that the plunderer would be plundered (Isaiah 33:1; Habakkuk 2:8). The Babylonian Chronicle says the conquerors carried off the vast booty of the city and the temple. Nineveh's palaces held the wealth of a hundred years of conquest, from Egypt to Elam; Ashurbanipal's own annals list the spoils of Thebes. The command is a call to the attackers to take, with the roles reversed: the city that sold nations (3:4) is itself now taken. The "storeroom" in the Plain English Translation is tekunah (see the variant). The word means "arrangement" in Ezekiel 43:11 and "place" in Job 23:3, and the Hebrew word list this site uses glosses it "supply" here. The Plain English Translation takes it as a place where supplies are laid out; "stock" or "supply" is the main alternative.

p: Qibbetsu pa'rur is the same phrase as Joel 2:6. Its exact meaning is debated.
b: The Hebrew qibbetsu pa'rur is literally "gathered pa'rur." The phrase also occurs in Joel 2:6, where this Plain English Translation says "Every face loses its color," and the Plain English Translation matches. The meaning of pa'rur is unclear. Proposals: "glow" (the flush of fear), "pallor" (the face turns pale, matching Joel's "loses its color"), or "a blackened pot" (parur, as the Greek reads: the face goes black like a cooking pot). Ancient readers understood fear in the face either way. The three-word verse opening ("empty, emptied, wasted away") is a sound play in Hebrew (buqah u-mevuqah u-mevullaqah) that English cannot match; Isaiah 24:1 has the same play.

p: Assyrian kings were pictured as lions. Nahum uses four lion words in three verses.
b: Lions were the Assyrian king's emblem. Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh had carved stone reliefs of royal lion hunts (now in the British Museum), and pairs of lions guarded gates. The Hebrew uses several lion words: 'aryeh (lion), lavi' (lioness), kefir (young lion), gur (cub). The Plain English Translation keeps four of them apart and uses "lionesses" for the plural lavi'ot in 2:12. Jeremiah 50:17 uses the same picture of Assyria's earlier devouring of Israel: "First the king of Assyria ate him up." The question "Where is the lions' lair now?" is a funeral cry (a form like "Where is the clerk? Where is the man with the scales?" in Isaiah 33:18).

a: The lion tore up what his cubs needed
t: The Lion of Wrath in the Nahum Pesher
p: A Qumran commentary on Nahum applies the lion passage to a later ruler, naming historical figures.
b: The Nahum Pesher (4QpNah, 4Q169), a commentary found at Qumran, copied in the first century BC, quotes Nahum and explains it, line by line, as being about events in its own time. Its comment on the lion who "tears prey for his cubs" names the "Lion of Wrath," who "hangs men alive"; most scholars identify him as the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (reigned 103-76 BC), who crucified hundreds of his opponents. Elsewhere it names "Demetrius king of Greece" and "Antiochus." These are the Qumran community's readings, not the Plain English Translation's, and the site's Dead Sea Scrolls printout for Nahum carries only Mur88 and 4QXIIg, not the pesher, so the identifications here follow the published editions (Allegro, DJD V; Horgan).

t: "Look, I am against you" and the LORD of Armies
p: A fixed challenge formula, used against Nineveh here and in 3:5, and against other cities elsewhere.
b: Hinni 'elayikh, "Look, I am against you," is a formula of challenge, the opening of a duel. It is used by the LORD against Babylon (Jeremiah 50:31; 51:25), Egypt (Ezekiel 29:3), Tyre (Ezekiel 26:3) and other powers. Nahum repeats it at 3:5, so the book's two halves each end an accusation with the same words. The title YHWH tseva'ot is rendered "the LORD of Armies"; "armies" may mean Israel's forces, the heavenly host or the stars, and the title includes the divine warrior. Here the shift from "her chariots" to "your young lions" in the Hebrew shows the oracle turning to speak to the city directly. The "messengers" of the last line are Assyria's envoys, like those Sennacherib sent to Hezekiah (2 Kings 19:9-14); they are the opposite of the herald of 1:15.
orig: הִנְנִי אֵלַיִךְ נְאֻם יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (hinni elayikh ne'um YHWH tseva'ot)

p: Hoy is the cry heard at a funeral. A prophet who says it is already mourning the one he addresses.
b: Hoy is rendered "Woe to" in the Plain English Translation. It was the cry at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30: "Oh, my brother!"), and a prophet who began a speech with it spoke as if the city were already dead. The same cry opens oracles in Isaiah 5, Amos 5:18 and 6:1, Habakkuk 2 and Zephaniah 2:5; and Zephaniah 3:1. The sorrow is part of the word, and a reader should keep both the threat and the mourning in mind, as the Plain English Translation does in Amos.

p: The Hebrew 'ir damim is used for Jerusalem in Ezekiel; Nahum uses it for Nineveh.
b: 'Ir damim is "city of bloods," the plural meaning acts of killing, not only blood. The Plain English Translation's "city of bloodshed" matches Ezekiel 22:2 and 24:6, 9, where the same phrase is said of Jerusalem. The charge is the same for both cities: violence that the LORD sees, and the title shows that the prophets used a single set of terms for cities that had lost their right to stand. Assyria's own kings recorded their cruelty in royal inscriptions (flayings, impalements, deportations), and Nahum's accusation is that the empire's blood was on the city (3:19 repeats this).

t: "City of Ephraim" in the Nahum Pesher
p: The Nahum Pesher takes 3:1-4 to be about a city of "the seekers of smooth things."
b: In the Nahum Pesher (4Q169, a Qumran commentary of the first century BC) the "city of bloodshed" is the city of Ephraim, the seekers of "smooth things" (usually taken to be the Pharisees), who walk in lies. This is how the Qumran community read the passage, and it shows that Nahum was applied to local politics 500 years after Nineveh. It is a reception of the book. The Plain English Translation does not follow it, and the site's printout of the Dead Sea Scrolls for Nahum does not include 4Q169, so the details are from the published editions.

a: acts of prostitution of the prostitute
p: The usual reading takes prostitution here as trade and politics. Hosea, Isaiah and Revelation use the image differently.
b: Zenunim ("acts of prostitution") is the Plain English Translation's word for it everywhere (Hosea 1:2; 4:10-18). In Hosea the image is Israel's unfaithfulness to the LORD. Here the usual reading is different: Nineveh "sells nations" through seduction, alliances and trade. Isaiah 23:15-17 uses the same picture of Tyre, a trading city that "sells herself to every kingdom." Other commentators hear a cultic side as well, because the same verse has "sorceries" (see the next note). Revelation 17-18 pictures Babylon the same way ("by your magic all the nations were led astray," Revelation 18:23), and Revelation 17:16 has the beast hate and strip the prostitute. The Greek of Nahum has the same word (porneia) as Revelation. These are shared images, not a claim that the passages describe the same city. The image of a city as a woman is old and has a long afterlife; its violence is dealt with at 3:5.

p: The two words come together in 2 Kings 9:22 (Jezebel); Isaiah 47 has sorceries for Babylon.
b: Ba'alat keshafim is "owner of sorceries." The pair "prostitution and sorceries" is in Jehu's words about Jezebel (2 Kings 9:22), and Isaiah 47:9, 12 says Babylon will fall "for all your many sorceries." Law forbids sorcery (Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10). In Nineveh itself, kings relied on diviners and exorcists, and the library of Ashurbanipal held thousands of omen texts, so the charge has a factual base: Assyrian policy was steered by omens. The Greek translates the word as pharmaka (drugs, spells), the source of the English "pharmacy."

a: I will uncover your skirts over your face
t: The woman shamed: a hard passage (3:5-7)
p: The city is pictured as a woman stripped in public by the LORD. Readers disagree whether this can be defended.
b: The picture is of a woman whose skirts are lifted over her face, who is made to be seen naked by nations, pelted with filth and left a spectacle (3:5-6). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and does not soften or defend it. The speaker is the LORD in the first person ("I will uncover," "I will hurl"), so the text gives the act a divine author. The same image is used of Judah in Jeremiah 13:26 and Ezekiel 16:37, of Israel in Hosea 2:10, and of Babylon in Isaiah 47:3. Critics (Weems, Yee, Julia O'Brien) say the prophets use sexual humiliation and violence against a female figure, with God as the agent, and ask whether this makes such acts holy. Others say it is a stock picture from ancient warfare, where the stripping of a captured city's women was a real part of conquest, and that the shame falls on the city as aggressor. Either way the passage is about conquest, in which the violation of women was real.
orig: וְגִלֵּיתִי שׁוּלַיִךְ עַל פָּנָיִךְ (ve-gillati shulayikh 'al panayikh)

a: make the nations look at your nakedness
t: Nakedness and shame; who defends the image
p: The Plain English Translation keeps nakedness and shame apart. Its Jeremiah 13:26 words the same Hebrew phrase differently.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps 'ervah "nakedness" and qalon "shame" apart here (Isaiah 47:3 has "nakedness" and "disgrace" for 'ervah and cherpah). The Plain English Translation's Jeremiah 13:26 has "strip off your skirts to your face" where Nahum says "uncover your skirts over your face"; the Hebrew phrase after the verb is the same ('al panayikh), and the two English wordings differ. Ortlund's Whoredom (1996) defends the marriage metaphor within a theology of God's unfaithful wife, writing on Hosea and the prophets in general. Alice Keefe (2001), writing on Hosea, reads the woman's body as a figure for the social body of the nation. Neither writes on Nahum; they are cited for how the image is read in the prophets.
orig: וְהַרְאֵיתִי גוֹיִם מַעְרֵךְ וּמַמְלָכוֹת קְלוֹנֵךְ (ve-har'eti goyim ma'erekh umamlakhot qelonekh)

p: Shiqqutsim usually means idols. Here it is things thrown at the city. The humiliation uses its own gods.
b: Shiqqutsim is the Bible's strong word for idols and what goes with them (Deuteronomy 29:17; 1 Kings 11:5; Daniel's "abomination that desolates"). English versions often make it "filth" here, and the sense is that of garbage thrown at someone shamed in public. In Nahum the choice of the word is a pointed one: the gods Nineveh trusted are what the LORD throws at her. The next word, nibbaltikh, "I will treat you with contempt" or "as a fool," is from nabal, the "godless fool." The Plain English Translation's "hold you in scorn" keeps the contempt.

p: The prophet's name means "comfort" (nacham). The same root is "change his mind" in Jonah, and not here.
b: Menachamim, "comforters," comes from nacham, the root of the name Nachum. The book named "Comfort" finds no comforter for Nineveh. The same root, in another form, is the verb the Plain English Translation renders "change his mind" when the LORD does so in Jonah 3:10 and Joel 2:13; so the book asks, without saying so, whether the God who "changed his mind about the harm" for Nineveh in Jonah's day will do so again. Nahum gives no answer in that sense: the Plain English Translation's last line, "Where would I look for comforters for you?" is a question with no reply. Lamentations 1:2, 9 and 17 say of Jerusalem that she has "no one to comfort her," a nearly identical phrase; Isaiah 40:1 begins the good news with "Comfort, comfort my people."

t: The ruin of Nineveh, Jonah and Tobit
p: Jonah said Nineveh would be "overturned"; Nahum says "ruined." Tobit 14 also tells of its fall.
b: Jonah's five words, "Nineveh will be overturned" (Jonah 3:4), were not carried out in his day because the city turned back (Jonah 3:10). Nahum's word for the final fall is shuddedah, "it is ruined." Tobit 14, a deuterocanonical book (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), has the dying Tobit tell his son to leave Nineveh because the prophets' word on it will come true. The Greek manuscripts differ on the prophet he names. Codex Sinaiticus has Nahum, and Codex Vaticanus has "Jonah the prophet" and names Jonah again in 14:8 (both as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus is usually reported with Vaticanus). The site's Tobit follows Sinaiticus: "the things Nahum spoke" (Tobit 14:4). See the variant there. Zephaniah 2:13-15 also foretells Nineveh's ruin. Reading Nahum with Jonah, as many of the Twelve's editors did, shows two words on one city: a pardon that lasted a generation or two, and a later end.

p: Thebes was Egypt's great southern city. Ashurbanipal sacked it about 663 BC, which dates the book after that.
b: The Hebrew is No' 'Amon, "city of Amun" (Amun was Thebes' chief god; Thebes is Greek). Jeremiah 46:25 and Ezekiel 30:14-16 mention it with the same Hebrew name. About 663 BC Ashurbanipal's army took Thebes from the Cushite king Tantamani and plundered its temples, and Ashurbanipal's own annals list its spoils. Nahum's question, "Are you any better than Thebes?" shows that it was already a fallen city, so Nahum was written after 663 BC. The question is whether it is much after: the commonest estimates put the book between 663 and 612 BC (see the book page). Thebes recovered under the Saite kings; Nineveh did not.

p: Ye'orim is an Egyptian loan word for the Nile and its arms. The Hebrew also calls the Nile "the sea."
b: Ye'or is from the Egyptian iteru, "river," and means the Nile (Exodus 1:22; Isaiah 19:5-8). Its plural ye'orim means the Nile's branches and canals; the Delta had many, and Thebes in Upper Egypt sat on the river. The Hebrew also calls the Nile "sea" (yam), as Isaiah 19:5 does: "The water will drain from the sea." So "her outer defense the sea" means the Nile. The Plain English Translation explains "the Nile's streams" for a reader who does not know the loan word. Nineveh had rivers and canals of its own (2:6), so the comparison is exact: water protected Thebes, as it was meant to protect Nineveh.

a: Her strength was Cush and Egypt
p: Thebes' allies were Nubia (Cush), the rest of Egypt, and peoples to the west. They did not save her.
b: Cush is Nubia, south of Egypt (Isaiah 18:1; the Cushite pharaohs of the 25th Dynasty ruled Egypt until the Assyrians drove them out in the 660s BC). Put and the Libyans were peoples west of the Nile; Put may be Libya or Punt (a name for a southern land) and is joined with Cush in Jeremiah 46:9 and Ezekiel 30:5. The Greek reads "Ethiopia," the usual Greek name for Cush. The point is that all of Thebes' resources were not enough. Tirhakah (Taharqa) of Cush fought Assyria in Hezekiah's day (2 Kings 19:9), and the Assyrians did overrun Egypt in 671 and 663 BC.

t: The smashed children: Nahum, Hosea, Psalm 137
p: The Plain English Translation's "smashed" matches 2 Kings 8:12 and Hosea 13:16 (same Hebrew verb). The cruelty is described, not softened.
b: The verb ratash, "smash" (H7376), is the same Hebrew verb as in 2 Kings 8:12 ("Their little ones you will smash"), Hosea 13:16 ("Their little ones will be smashed") and Isaiah 13:16, where the Plain English Translation has "battered to pieces" for the same root. Psalm 137:9 wishes a like fate on Babylon's babies, with a different verb ("shatters"). The Hebrew of 3:10 names no one who does the smashing; that it was Assyria's army is the usual inference from the fall of Thebes (about 663 BC), not a statement of the text. The moral problem is the same wherever it is found. In Hosea 13:16 the smashing of Samaria's little ones is announced as the LORD's own judgment ("Samaria will be held guilty"), and in 2 Kings 8:12 Elisha weeps because he knows what Hazael will do to Israel. So the Bible reports this cruelty both as the deed of enemies and as the judgment of God, and does not hide the difficulty. Nahum does not say that Nineveh's children will be smashed; what it says of Nineveh's fate is in 3:5-7 and 3:11-19. A reader should hold this verse beside Psalm 137:9 and Hosea 13:16.

a: They cast lots for her honored men
p: Lots decided who got which prisoner. Joel and Obadiah say the same of Jerusalem.
b: Captives were divided among the victors by lot. Joel 3:3 and Obadiah 11 say of Jerusalem that "they cast lots" for its people. In Nahum the same happens to Thebes' nobles. The pattern is the same for Judah and for Egypt, and Nahum warns Nineveh of the same. The Hebrew yadu goral is the standard phrase for a lot cast (see the topic on casting lots).

p: Drunkenness is the picture of a nation that has drunk God's anger and cannot stand.
b: In the prophets the LORD hands nations a cup that makes them stagger (Jeremiah 25:15-29; Isaiah 51:17-23; Habakkuk 2:15-16; Obadiah 16). Lamentations 4:21 tells Edom, "The cup is coming around to you too; you will get drunk and expose yourself," which joins drunkenness to nakedness; Nahum has the shaming of 3:5-7 and the drunkenness of 3:11 in one poem. Jeremiah 51:39 has Babylon's leaders drunk and asleep "an endless sleep." The word "too" in Nahum answers the comparison with Thebes: she drank it, and so will Nineveh.

a: Each of your fortresses is a fig tree with early figs
p: The first figs are so ripe that a shake drops them into the eater's mouth. Isaiah 28:4 has the picture.
b: Bikkurim are the first-ripe figs, which fall at a touch. Isaiah 28:4 uses the picture for Samaria: "like the first fig of the year, ripe before summer: the one who spots it gulps it down while it is still in his hand." Hosea 9:10 and Micah 7:1 give figs different meanings. Nineveh's fortresses, outer forts on the roads to the capital, are the figs that Nineveh's boast made look strong but that the enemy shakes down in a night. The Babylonian Chronicle reports that towns near Nineveh, such as Tarbisu and then Ashur, fell in 614 BC, before the capital.

t: "Your people are women": a stock curse
p: Treaty curses threatened that a covenant-breaker's soldiers would become women. Nahum uses it as a taunt.
b: The Hebrew is 'ammekh, "your people." The word 'am can mean the people as a whole or the fighting men; the Plain English Translation says "people" and leaves the choice open. The context (an enemy at the gates, bars burned) suggests fighting men, as in Jeremiah 50:37 and 51:30. Calling an army "women" was a standard insult and a treaty curse in the ancient Near East (Delbert Hillers, Treaty-Curses and the Old Testament Prophets, 1964, collected the parallels, including Jeremiah 50:37 and 51:30 and Nahum 3:13). Isaiah 19:16 says the same of Egypt. The taunt uses women as the picture of weakness, which many modern readers reject. The Plain English Translation reports it and does not defend or soften it. The fault named is the people's or the army's, not women's, but the word depends on a view of women that the text assumes and does not question.

a: fire will eat up your bars
p: Excavators report fire and fighting at Nineveh's gates, which fits the text without proving any detail.
b: Excavations at Nineveh's gates (Thompson and Hutchinson in the 1920s and 1930s, and later work reviewed by Stronach) found burning and signs of fighting at some of the gates and in the palaces. This fits the Chronicle's report that the city was sacked and burned. Whether the "bars" of Nahum are the wooden bars of the gates or the bolts of fortress doors is unclear. Jeremiah 51:30 uses nearly the same words of Babylon ("her bolts are snapped"). The Plain English Translation says "gates of your land," which in Hebrew can mean the passes into the land and the gates of its towns.

a: It will eat you up like the hopping locust
p: Nahum uses yeleq, 'arbeh and a swarm word. The Plain English Translation keeps Joel's wording for yeleq.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps Joel 1:4's four locust words apart there. In Nahum 3:15-17 the words are yeleq (3:15, 16), 'arbeh (3:15, 17) and gov gevai (3:17, "a swarm of locusts," matching Amos 7:1). So yeleq is "the hopping locust" as in Joel 1:4 and 2:25, 'arbeh is plain "locust" as in Exodus 10 (the Plain English Translation says "swarming locust" for it only in Joel 1:4 and 2:25, where Joel's four names are kept apart), and the swarm is "a swarm of locusts." The irony of 3:15 has two readings: the fire and sword will eat Nineveh as locusts eat a field, and Nineveh is told to "multiply" like locusts, which will not help. The command to multiply ironically describes the city's many merchants, officials and soldiers, who vanish like locusts (3:16-17).

t: Does the locust strip, or molt?
p: The verb pashat means to strip off. The locust sheds its skin, or strips the land, then flies.
b: Pashat is "strip, take off" (a robe, Genesis 37:23; skin, Leviticus 1:6). Two readings: (1) the young hopper sheds its skin and then flies away on new wings, a natural-history observation that the city's riches take wing; (2) the locust strips the land and moves on. The Plain English Translation takes the second, since the verse is about a swarm that takes everything and goes. Either way the point is the same: the merchants, like locusts, were many and left no loyalty.

a: camping along the walls on a cold day
p: On a cold morning locusts cling still to walls. When the sun warms them they fly. So the officials vanish.
b: Locusts stay on walls and hedges through the chill of night and early morning, and fly when the sun warms them. Nahum uses this for the officials and scribes of Nineveh: they gather around the city in the cool and are gone at the first heat of the day. The "court officers" (minnazarayikh) and "scribes" (tapsarayikh) may be loan words from Akkadian: tapsar seems to come from tupsharru, "scribe"; the first title is less sure. Between them Mur88 and 4QXIIg keep both words in readable letters.

p: Shepherd is the Near Eastern word for king and ruler. Sleep means death here, as in Jeremiah 51.
b: Kings in Mesopotamia and Israel were "shepherds" of their people (2 Samuel 5:2; Jeremiah 23:1-4; Ezekiel 34). In the poem, the king's helpers are asleep at their post, and in the Old Testament "sleep" is also the word for death (Psalm 76:5-6; Jeremiah 51:39, 57). The Greek makes the king of Assyria the one who puts the nobles to sleep (see the variant). If the shepherds sleep, the flock is scattered on the hills, and "no one is there to gather" them (compare Ezekiel 34:5-6, where Israel's flock is scattered because the shepherds failed).

p: Nahum never names a king. Ashurbanipal ruled until about 631 BC, and four more kings followed before the end.
b: Assyrian kings in the years Nahum may have in view: Ashurbanipal (669 to about 631 BC), Ashur-etil-ilani, Sin-shumu-lishir, and Sin-shar-ishkun, who died at the fall of Nineveh in 612 (the Chronicle says he "died" at the time); Ashur-uballit II then held out at Harran until about 609. Nahum names none of them, and the date of the book rests on Thebes (663) and the fall (612) and on how the prophet describes Assyria's strength. Zephaniah 2:13-15, in Josiah's day, foretells the same end in nearly the same terms. The "king" is the empire's throne, not any one man.

t: The last words: Nahum answers Jonah
p: Jonah ends with a question about pity for Nineveh. Nahum ends with a question about its wickedness.
b: The Hebrew ra'ah, "wickedness" or "evil," is the word God uses in Jonah 1:2: "their wickedness has come up in front of me." Nahum 3:19 ends on it: "For is there anyone your wickedness has not passed over, again and again?" Jonah 4:11 ends with a question God asks the prophet: should I not have pity on Nineveh? The two questions fit like a pair, and in both the Hebrew and the Greek order of the Twelve Jonah comes before Nahum. The Hebrew of both is an open question: neither book answers it aloud. A reader who sets the two side by side sees that the book of Jonah asks whether Nineveh deserves mercy and Nahum recalls what the city did with the mercy it was given.
orig: כִּי עַל מִי לֹא עָבְרָה רָעָתְךָ תָּמִיד (ki 'al mi lo avrah ra'atekha tamid)

a: There is no relief for your fracture
p: Nahum uses Jeremiah's words about Zion's wound for Nineveh's.
b: Jeremiah 30:12 says of Zion, "Your fracture is past healing; your wound is severe." Nahum 3:19 says of Nineveh, "There is no relief for your fracture. Your wound is severe," with the same Hebrew for "fracture" (sheber) and "your wound is severe" (nachlah makkatekh). Whether Nahum used Jeremiah, Jeremiah used Nahum, or both used a common lament is not settled. Jeremiah 10:19 and 15:18 use similar words for Jeremiah's own suffering. The point is the reversal: the words that were Zion's lament over a hurt that would not heal become the LORD's judgment on Nineveh's hurt.
